sections.html:
• Other names: Spotted porcelain crab, Porcelain Crab, Anemone crab
  • Synonyms: Neopetrolisthes ohshimai, Petrolisthes ohshimai, Porcellana maculata
  • Minimum tank size: 20 litres
  • Keeping: easy; breeding: difficult
  • Size (carapace): up to 2.5 cm
  • Water type: SG 1.020–1.025
  • KH: 7–12
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: mostly carnivore / omnivore
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Colour: creamy white with a number of small red/purple spots and/or blotches

Porcellanidae, the porcelain crabs, are a family of decapods in the infraorder Anomura, so porcelain anemone crabs are not true crabs. They superficially resemble true crabs and have flattened bodies adapted to living in crevices and under rocks, but are more closely related to hermit crabs. Unlike true crabs, the abdomen of Neopetrolisthes maculatus still retains a tail fan similar to that of lobsters or shrimp.

Some aquarists keep these crabs without anemones, believing they can live on live rock or corals. They cannot: porcelain anemone crabs evolved to succeed only when living with anemones. Without one they feel vulnerable and become stressed, and under constant stress they die much faster, even in an aquarium with good water parameters.

Every porcelain anemone crab sold in a pet store has been captured in the wild. Do not keep them without an anemone; if you cannot provide one, do not buy them.

Widely distributed in the Indo-West Pacific, from the east coast of Africa (Zanzibar, Mozambique, Madagascar) to Christmas Island and Western Australia, Bismarck Archipelago, Queensland, Moluccas, Palau, Taiwan, Southern Japan (Ryukyu Islands), New Caledonia, and the Marshall and Fiji Islands.

There is a lot of confusion over the taxonomy of these crabs, and the scientific names given by aquarium stores are often wrong. Neopetrolisthes maculatus and Neopetrolisthes ohshimai are not two different species. The Indian and Pacific Ocean populations have different spot patterns, but they cannot be distinguished by other morphological characters, so biologists prefer to treat Neopetrolisthes ohshimai under the name Neopetrolisthes maculatus.

In nature, porcelain anemone crabs are commonly found on rocky and coral reefs of temperate and tropical coasts, and are among the common crustaceans of tropical and subtropical shallow subtidal waters. Neopetrolisthes maculatus often lives on sea anemones and is collected at depths of 5 to 12 metres.

They live in a symbiotic relationship with anemones. The anemones protect the crabs from predators by providing shelter, while the crabs clean the host anemone by eating food scraps and mucus off its body surface. Resistance to the toxins and the production of mucus that prevents the anemone from stinging them allow them to live together. Because of this relationship, anemone crabs are almost never found deeper than 12 metres. They are relatively slow-moving and cannot survive in the ocean without the anemone's protection.

Neopetrolisthes maculatus has been found in association with several genera of sea anemones, for example:

  • Stichodactyla spp.
  • Cryptodendrum adhaesivum
  • Gyrostoma
  • Telmatactis cricoides
  • Macrodactyla doreensis
  • Phymanthus sp.
  • Heteractis spp.
  • Actinodendron plumosum
  • Anemonia sulcata
  • Zoanthus sp.
  • Lebrunia danae
  • Entacmaea quadricolor

The crabs spend most of their time close to the anemone's tentacles, on the column, and occasionally even on the tentacles and oral disk. Contact between the crab and the tentacles does not stimulate the anemone's feeding reaction; the tentacles do not cling to the crab and the crab shows no signs of being stung.

Depending on the other livestock, a small tank (20 litres) can be enough for a pair of porcelain anemone crabs. Ideally, use a 40-litre tank. A bigger tank also helps reduce fluctuations in water quality.

Porcelain anemone crabs are hardy, undemanding and easy to care for, which is why they are quite popular in the hobby. Prepare for their arrival beforehand so you can meet their needs.

Like other crustaceans, they shed their exoskeleton (moult) as they grow, and the frequency depends on the crab's age. Do not touch the crab at this stage, as it is very vulnerable and may die if disturbed. Before moulting, activity and feeding decrease. During moulting the crab absorbs a lot of water until the carapace splits at a breaking point, then wriggles out of the old shell through this opening. The new, larger exoskeleton takes at least a few hours to harden. Sometimes the crab leaves its anemone and hides in the rocks, so do not worry too much if you cannot find it.

Anemone crabs are fairly adaptable to a wide range of water parameters, but they still have preferences.

  • Temperature: about 22 to 31°C, with 24–27°C optimal. Install a heater and thermometer to keep the temperature constant.
  • pH: 8.1 to 8.4
  • Alkalinity: 7 to 12 dKH, although values often go a little higher or lower
  • Specific gravity: 1.021 to 1.026

Ammonia is the biggest risk in any hard-water aquarium. In a reef tank, many fish, shrimp and crabs die young because water parameters are not kept stable beyond a couple of months. Check water conditions often: the sooner a problem is found, the easier it is to correct.

As filter feeders, they like strong water flow. Filtration should be robust.

Lighting should be adapted to the needs of the symbiotic sea anemones. Anemones usually house photosynthetic microorganisms that provide them with energy, so light improves their overall health and colour.

Anemones are harder to keep than anemone crabs, so if you want to keep the two together, the tank must be designed around the anemone first. Beginners are advised to avoid anemones until they are a little more experienced, but the crabs need anemones for their well-being. After purchase, follow proper acclimation steps before introducing the animal to the tank. Acclimate very slowly, as with all invertebrates; 2–3 hours is generally enough.

Porcelain anemone crabs are active filter feeders. They use fans on their mouthparts (plume-like bristles, the third maxillipeds) to feed on particles such as plankton suspended in the water column. Water movement delivers food and oxygen while removing waste products.

Unlike freshwater filter-feeding shrimp (such as bamboo shrimp or vampire shrimp), they can also use their claws to feed, so they scavenge (algae, detritus) too. They also eat mucus from the anemone. They are omnivores and can be part of a clean-up crew.

In aquariums they get their share when you feed corals. Spraying a little food over the top of the crab will make it happy. They fan all the time and do fine on leftover food.

Diet includes:

  • mysis
  • brine shrimp
  • rotifers
  • bloodworms
  • phytoplankton
  • zooplankton
  • marine snow
  • flakes
  • spirulina
  • pieces of meaty food
  • fish or shrimp food
  • meat-based pellets
  • whatever they can catch in their fans

Porcelain anemone crabs have a very peaceful temperament. They fight only when someone tries to bully them out of their anemone. They occur as a male/female pair (the male is smaller than the female) on a sea anemone, and the pair will not tolerate their own species on the same host. They spend most of the daylight hours sitting in the anemone, putting out their fans to filter food from the surrounding water.

They have large, flattened front claws that look frightening, but are used only in territorial fights with their own species, not for hunting; usually they simply shove other crabs away. The long transparent antennae are always directed to the sides. The legs are rather short, and unlike most crabs they use only three pairs of legs for walking (the fourth pair is hidden under the carapace). The compressed body helps them stay in position in turbulent water.

Being small and less able to defend themselves, these crabs can voluntarily shed a limb or body part (autotomy) to limit damage and escape predation.

Tankmates: they are harmless to other community tank members and are reef safe, not damaging anything in a reef tank. They fight over anemones, so if you keep more than two in a tank, you need several anemones. Anemone crabs often do not chase away 'Sexy' shrimp, which also need anemones. Do not keep them with bullies, especially clownfish, which will try to take the anemone and usually win. Peppermint shrimp, red fire shrimp, skunk cleaner shrimp and harlequin shrimp are peaceful options. Boxer crabs, bumblebee shrimp, snails (cerith, bumblebee, conch, nassarius), other porcelain crabs, emerald crabs and hermit crabs (Halloween, blue leg) usually do not bother them. Do not keep them with aggressive fish such as groupers, lionfish, eels and triggerfish, which will prey on them.

Sexing is somewhat tricky. Some aquarists believe the spots of the female are red and those of the male purple, and that the spots on the carapace are sparser, larger and more irregular in the female. However, biologists have reported that colour differences are not related to sex, and male/female pairs of similar coloration have been found on the same host.

According to studies, sex can be determined by the pleopods: males have a pair of developed pleopods on the second abdominal somite, while the pleopods on the third to fifth somites are each reduced to a small, rounded, inconspicuous rudiment with a small pore. Females have pairs of developed pleopods on the third to fifth abdominal somites, those on the fourth and fifth somites being large. Unless you are a biologist, this is very difficult.

Breeding is difficult. So far there have been no reports of successful breeding of porcelain anemone crabs in captivity. Even biologists have not achieved it; their most successful attempt reached the second zoea stage.

In the rearing experiment with Neopetrolisthes maculatus:

  • Filtered seawater from the collection site was used.
  • Water temperature and salinity were kept at 29.0–29.5°C and 34.0–35.0%.
  • Zoeae were fed daily with newly hatched Artemia nauplii.
  • Larval excrement was removed with a pipette.
  • The water in each rearing vessel was kept at a constant level by adding seawater.

The larvae passed through two zoeal stages but died before moulting to the next phase (megalopa). The stage lasted 5–7 days. First zoea size: 2.1–2.3 mm; second zoea size: 2.8–3.1 mm.

  • The eggs are usually reddish-brown.
  • Females can carry around 600 eggs.
  • The eggs hatch as free-swimming zoeae that feed on plankton.
  • Larval development of porcellanids usually consists of two zoeal stages and one megalopal stage.

Porcelain anemone crabs are a spotted crab with two colour forms: in one, the carapace, claws and legs are white with an uneven pattern of red blotches of irregular size; in the other, they have a uniform pattern of numerous small reddish-purple spots. Fully grown, the leg span reaches 6–8 cm, while carapace length is usually 2.5–3 cm. Under optimal conditions they can live 3–5 years.
